title: God has decreed to concur whenever the will determines itself; the kind of act comes from the will
source_text: XXXII. Quamvis vero Voluntas, sine Deo concurrente, nihil omnino possit, ex lege tamen a Deo, dum liberam illam condidit, constituta, concursus ille semper ipsi praesto est, quia Deus voluit, & ab aeterno decrevit ad omne opus liberae voluntatis concurrere, quando ad operandum ipsa se determinaverit. Nec minus eadem Voluntas libera est quoad actus sui specificationem. Quod enim voluntas bene vel male agit, istud potius fugit quam appetit, ex vi quadam divini concursus non procedit, sed ex propria Voluntatis determinatione, quae ad hujus potius quam alterius speciei actionem edendam, concursu divino ex se indifferenti libere utitur.
pass_a_gloss: But although the Will, without God concurring, can do nothing at all, yet by the law established by God, when he made it free, that concurrence is always at hand to it, because God willed, and from eternity decreed to concur to every work of the free will, when it has determined itself to operating. Nor is the same Will less free as to the specification of its act. For that the will acts well or ill, that it rather flees than seeks, does not proceed from some force of the divine concurrence, but from the proper determination of the Will, which for putting forth an action of this rather than of another species, freely uses the divine concurrence indifferent of itself.
pass_b_english: The will can do nothing at all without God's concurrence. Yet under the law God laid down when he made it free, that concurrence is always ready for it, because God willed, and decreed from eternity, to concur in every work of the free will once the will has determined itself to act.

The will is no less free as to the specification of its act. Whether it acts well or badly, whether it shuns a thing rather than seeks it, does not come from any force in the divine concurrence but from the will's own determination. In producing an action of this kind rather than that, the will freely makes use of God's concurrence, which of itself is indifferent.

lemmas.gloss: is always at hand to it
the divine concurrence indifferent of itself

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.
